claim: TibC from ETEC harbors a heptosyltransferase activity on TibA and AIDA-I.
source: Here we demonstrate that TibC from ETEC harbors a heptosyltransferase activity on TibA and AIDA-I, defining a large family of bacterial autotransporter heptosyltransferases (BAHTs).
evidence: Demonstrated through co-expression experiments showing glycosylation of AIDA-I and TibA by TibC (Figure 1B, C), mass spectrometry analysis showing heptose modifications (Figure 1G), and in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 1I).

claim: TibC defines a large family of bacterial autotransporter heptosyltransferases (BAHTs).
source: Here we demonstrate that TibC from ETEC harbors a heptosyltransferase activity on TibA and AIDA-I, defining a large family of bacterial autotransporter heptosyltransferases (BAHTs).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment showing homologues in multiple bacterial species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and reference to parallel study (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: The crystal structure of TibC reveals a characteristic ring-shape dodecamer.
source: The crystal structure of TibC reveals a characteristic ring-shape dodecamer.
evidence: Demonstrated by X-ray crystallography at 2.9 Å resolution (Table 1) and confirmed by cryo-EM at 11.5 Å resolution (Figure 2C).

claim: The TibC protomer features an N-terminal β-barrel, a catalytic domain, a β-hairpin thumb, and a unique iron-finger motif.
source: The protomer features an N-terminal β-barrel, a catalytic domain, a β-hairpin thumb, and a unique iron-finger motif.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure and described in detail (Figure 3A).

claim: The iron-finger motif contributes to back-to-back dimerization.
source: The iron-finger motif contributes to back-to-back dimerization; six dimers form the ring through β-hairpin thumb-mediated hand-in-hand contact.
evidence: Structural analysis showing the iron-finger motif at the dimerization interface (Figure 5D) and functional validation showing iron-binding mutants fail to form dodecamers (Figure 5B).

claim: Six dimers form the ring through β-hairpin thumb-mediated hand-in-hand contact.
source: The iron-finger motif contributes to back-to-back dimerization; six dimers form the ring through β-hairpin thumb-mediated hand-in-hand contact.
evidence: Structural analysis showing β-hairpin thumb at hand-in-hand interface (Figure 4A) and mutations disrupting this contact prevent dodecamer formation (Figure 4B).

claim: The structure of ADP-D,D-heptose-bound TibC reveals a sugar transfer mechanism.
source: The structure of ADP-D-glycero-β-D-manno-heptose (ADP-D,D-heptose)-bound TibC reveals a sugar transfer mechanism and also the ligand stereoselectivity determinant.
evidence: Crystal structure of TibC D110A mutant soaked with ADP-D,D-heptose at 3.88 Å resolution showing ligand binding and catalytic residues (Figure 6B, Table 1).

claim: The ADP-D,D-heptose-bound TibC structure reveals the ligand stereoselectivity determinant.
source: The structure of ADP-D-glycero-β-D-manno-heptose (ADP-D,D-heptose)-bound TibC reveals a sugar transfer mechanism and also the ligand stereoselectivity determinant.
evidence: Structural analysis identifying Pro-300 as the stereoselectivity determinant (Figure 6E) and mutagenesis experiments swapping stereoselectivity (Figure 6C).

claim: Electron-cryomicroscopy analyses uncover a TibC–TibA dodecamer/hexamer assembly with two enzyme molecules binding to one TibA substrate.
source: Electron-cryomicroscopy analyses uncover a TibC–TibA dodecamer/hexamer assembly with two enzyme molecules binding to one TibA substrate.
evidence: Cryo-EM reconstruction at 8.2-8.9 Å resolution showing the complex structure (Figure 7A, C) and analytical ultracentrifugation determining molecular weight of 750 kDa consistent with TibC12-TibA6 stoichiometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The TibC dodecamer complex enables high efficient hyperglycosylation of six autotransporter substrates simultaneously.
source: The complex structure also highlights a high efficient hyperglycosylation of six autotransporter substrates simultaneously by the dodecamer enzyme complex.
evidence: Inferred from the cryo-EM structure showing six TibA molecules bound to the TibC dodecamer (Figure 7C) and the architectural arrangement.

claim: Co-expression of TibC or AAH together with AIDA-I in E. coli BL21 cells resulted in tight adhesion of the bacteria to HeLa cells.
source: Co-expression of TibC or AAH together with AIDA-I in E. coli BL21 cells resulted in a tight adhesion of the bacteria to HeLa cells (Figure 1A) and AIDA-I glycosylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy showing bacterial adhesion to HeLa cells (Figure 1A).

claim: Co-expression of TibC with AIDA-I results in AIDA-I glycosylation.
source: Co-expression of TibC or AAH together with AIDA-I in E. coli BL21 cells resulted in a tight adhesion of the bacteria to HeLa cells (Figure 1A) and AIDA-I glycosylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycoprotein detection assay (Figure 1B).

claim: Co-expression of TibC induced TibA glycosylation in the heterologous system.
source: Co-expression of TibC also induced TibA glycosylation in the heterologous system (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycoprotein detection assay (Figure 1C).

claim: TibA305-350 is a minimal passenger domain fragment of TibA that can be efficiently glycosylated by TibC.
source: We further identified a minimal passenger domain fragment of TibA (TibA305-350) that could be efficiently glycosylated by TibC (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycosylation assays of TibA truncations (Figure 1D, E).

claim: Co-expression of TibC with SUMO-Flag-TibA305-350-Flag resulted in mass increase of 576, 768, or 960 Da, corresponding to the addition of 3, 4, and 5 heptoses, respectively.
source: Co-expression of TibC resulted in mass increase of 576, 768, or 960 Da, corresponding to the addition of 3, 4, and 5 heptoses, respectively (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by ESI mass spectrometry analysis (Figure 1G).

claim: Serine residues (Ser-313 and Ser-322), but not threonine residues, are the modification sites in TibA by TibC.
source: Similarly to that performed with AAH modification of AIDA-I (Lu et al., 2014), serine residues (Ser-313 and Ser-322 within DK-305SASKVIQNSGGAVITNTSAAVSGTN329), but not threonine residues, were identified to be the modification sites by electron transfer dissociation (ETD) mass spectrometry (Figure 1H).
evidence: Identified by ETD mass spectrometry analysis (Figure 1H) and comparison with AAH modification pattern (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: Recombinant TibC directly modifies synthetic peptides derived from the passenger domains of either AIDA-I or TibA.
source: Supporting the heptosyltransferase activity of TibC, recombinant TibC was found to directly modify synthetic peptides derived from the passenger domains of either AIDA-I or TibA in which ADP-D,D-heptose, but not the anomer ADP-L,D-heptose, could serve as the sugar ligand (Figure 1I).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro enzymatic assays with MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (Figure 1I).

claim: ADP-D,D-heptose, but not the anomer ADP-L,D-heptose, can serve as the sugar ligand for TibC.
source: Supporting the heptosyltransferase activity of TibC, recombinant TibC was found to directly modify synthetic peptides derived from the passenger domains of either AIDA-I or TibA in which ADP-D,D-heptose, but not the anomer ADP-L,D-heptose, could serve as the sugar ligand (Figure 1I).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro enzymatic assays showing modification only with ADP-D,D-heptose (Figure 1I).

claim: AAH and TibC homologues are widely present in pathogenic bacteria species including Citrobacter rodentium, Salmonella enterica serovar Urbana, Shigella sp. D9, Laribacter hongkongensis, Cronobacter sakazakii, and several Burkholderia species.
source: AAH and TibC homologues, defined as the BAHT family (Lu et al., 2014), are widely present in pathogenic bacteria species including Citrobacter rodentium, Salmonella enterica serovar Urbana, Shigella sp. D9, Laribacter hongkongensis, Cronobacter sakazakii, and several Burkholderia species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and reference to parallel study (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: BAHT proteins generally bear more than 50% sequence homology to TibC/AAH.
source: These proteins generally bear more than 50% sequence homology to TibC/AAH and contain residues critical for the heptosyltransferase activity (see below).
evidence: Inferred from sequence alignment analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: In the genomic locus, genes encoding BAHT are often followed by an autotransporter or a putative autotransporter.
source: In the genomic locus, genes encoding BAHT are often followed by an autotransporter or a putative autotransporter, consistent with the notion that BAHT modifies its autotransporter partner for functioning (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from genomic analysis and cited from parallel study (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: The passenger domain of AIDA-I shows sequence similarities to that of TibA.
source: Consistent with the modification of AIDA-I by TibC, the passenger domain of AIDA-I shows sequence similarities to that of TibA and contains a number of heptosylation motifs identified in TibA previously (Lu et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and reference to previous identification of heptosylation motifs (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: The passenger domain of AIDA-I contains a number of heptosylation motifs identified in TibA previously.
source: Consistent with the modification of AIDA-I by TibC, the passenger domain of AIDA-I shows sequence similarities to that of TibA and contains a number of heptosylation motifs identified in TibA previously (Lu et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and cited from previous study (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: A TibC variant with three mutated epitopes (E83A/E84A, K400A/K401A, and Q215A/E216A) produced the highest quality crystal.
source: A number of point mutations designed to reduce the surface entropy were screened and a TibC variant with three mutated epitopes (E83A/E84A, K400A/K401A, and Q215A/E216A) produced the highest quality crystal.
evidence: Described as the approach used to obtain diffracting crystals for structure determination.

claim: The TibC mutant (E83A/E84A, K400A/K401A, Q215A/E216A) exhibited identical biochemical and biological functions to wild-type TibC.
source: This mutant exhibited identical biochemical and biological functions to wild-type TibC (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by functional assays showing equivalent activity (Figure 1A-C).

claim: A 2.9 Å structure of TibC was solved by single wavelength dispersion phasing using anomalous signals from selenomethionine and the naturally bound ferric ion.
source: A 2.9 Å structure was solved by single wavelength dispersion phasing using anomalous signals from selenomethionine (SeMet) and the naturally bound ferric ion (Table 1).
evidence: Described as the method used for structure determination with crystallographic statistics provided (Table 1).

claim: One asymmetric unit in the TibC structure contains 12 TibC molecules assembled into a large ring structure.
source: Strikingly, one asymmetric unit in the solved structure contains 12 TibC molecules, which are assembled into a large ring structure (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2A).

claim: The TibC dodecamer ring has an external diameter of 145 Å and a height of 72 Å.
source: The overall shape of the dodecamer ring resembles a circular garland with an external diameter of 145 Å and a height of 72 Å.
evidence: Measured from the crystal structure (Figure 2A).

claim: The TibC dodecamer has an inner diameter of approximately 110 Å.
source: Parts of the 12 protomers are lined side by side at the central plate to form the stem of the garland with an inner diameter of ∼110 Å (Figure 2A).
evidence: Measured from the crystal structure (Figure 2A).

claim: The inner surface of the TibC dodecamer stem is decorated with uniformly distributed 12 ferric ions, forming a characteristic iron belt along the ring.
source: The inner surface of the stem is decorated with uniformly distributed 12 ferric ions, forming a characteristic iron belt along the ring (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2A).

claim: The presence of ferric ions in TibC is expected from the brownish color of recombinant TibC protein in solution.
source: The presence of ferric ions is expected from the brownish color of recombinant TibC protein in solution.
evidence: Inferred from visual observation of protein color.

claim: Six symmetric TibC protomers project upwards from the central plate while the other six project downwards, generating a gear-like shape at both sides.
source: Six symmetric TibC protomers project upwards from the central plate while the other six project downwards, generating a gear-like shape at both sides.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2A).

claim: Two adjacent TibC protomers projecting oppositely contact each other in a back-to-back manner around a dyad axis.
source: Two adjacent TibC protomers projecting oppositely contact each other in a back-to-back manner around a dyad axis; six back-to-back dimers are further linked together in a hand-in-hand fashion around a sixfold axis to form the garland-like ring (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2B).

claim: Six back-to-back dimers are linked together in a hand-in-hand fashion around a sixfold axis to form the garland-like ring.
source: Two adjacent TibC protomers projecting oppositely contact each other in a back-to-back manner around a dyad axis; six back-to-back dimers are further linked together in a hand-in-hand fashion around a sixfold axis to form the garland-like ring (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2B).

claim: The dodecamer assembly can be viewed as a hexameric oligomerization of dimers.
source: Thus, the dodecamer assembly can be viewed as a hexameric oligomerization of dimers.
evidence: Inferred from the structural organization showing six dimers forming the dodecamer (Figure 2B).

claim: The back-to-back interface in TibC is extensive and tilts across the central plate by 45°.
source: The back-to-back interface is extensive and tilts across the central plate by 45° (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Measured from the crystal structure (Figure 2A, B).

claim: The hand-in-hand connection creates 12 tilted grooves extending to the interior of the garland from both up and down sides.
source: The hand-in-hand connection creates 12 tilted grooves extending to the interior of the garland from both up and down sides.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2A).

claim: Cryo-EM reconstruction of TibC at 11.5 Å resolution showed a remarkably similar dodecamer architecture to that determined by X-ray crystallography.
source: A 3D reconstruction of 11.5 Å was obtained from the cryo-EM images, which showed a remarkably similar dodecamer architecture to that determined by X-ray crystallography (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 2C) and comparison with crystal structure.

claim: The dodecamer ring architecture is the predominant form of TibC protein in solution and likely represents a functional physiological state.
source: This suggests that the dodecamer ring architecture is the predominant form of TibC protein in solution and likely represents a functional physiological state.
evidence: Inferred from cryo-EM showing dodecamer in solution (Figure 2C), gel filtration showing ~500 kDa oligomer, and analytical ultracentrifugation showing 578 kDa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Purified TibC eluted as an oligomer of approximately 500 kDa on the gel filtration column.
source: Consistently, purified TibC eluted as an oligomer of ∼500 kDa on the gel filtration column (see below) and the molecular weight was determined to be 578 kDa by analytic ultracentrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration chromatography.

claim: The molecular weight of TibC was determined to be 578 kDa by analytic ultracentrifugation.
source: Consistently, purified TibC eluted as an oligomer of ∼500 kDa on the gel filtration column (see below) and the molecular weight was determined to be 578 kDa by analytic ultracentrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by analytical ultracentrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: All 12 TibC protomers adopt an identical structure containing an N-terminal β-barrel domain, a core catalytic domain, a β-hairpin thumb, and an iron-finger motif arranged into a palm-like shape.
source: All the 12 TibC protomers adopt an identical structure containing an N-terminal β-barrel domain, a core catalytic domain, a β-hairpin thumb, and an iron-finger motif which are arranged into a palm-like shape (Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A).

claim: The β-hairpin thumb and the iron-finger motif are insertions into the catalytic domain.
source: The β-hairpin thumb and the iron-finger motif are insertions into the catalytic domain.
evidence: Inferred from the structural organization and domain architecture (Figure 3A).

claim: The TibC β-barrel is structured from two four-stranded sheets that pack against each other.
source: The flattened β-barrel (residues 1–97) is structured from two four-stranded sheets that pack against each other.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A).

claim: The TibC β-barrel is stacked against the catalytic domain from the side and makes extensive contacts with β9, β12, and the loop linking α3 and β12.
source: The barrel is stacked against the catalytic domain from the side and makes extensive contacts with β9, β12, and the loop linking α3 and β12; several hydrophobic residues from both domains are in close proximity at the interface (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The β-barrel is well separated from the catalytic domain and is unlikely to play a direct role in sugar transfer.
source: The β-barrel is well separated from the catalytic domain and is unlikely to play a direct role in sugar transfer.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis showing spatial separation from the catalytic site.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal 80 or 95 residues abolished TibC heptosylation of TibA.
source: Notably, deletion of the N-terminal 80 or 95 residues abolished TibC heptosylation of TibA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating a possible function of the β-barrel domain in either substrate recognition or maintaining structural integrity of the enzyme.
evidence: Demonstrated by glycosylation assays of TibC deletion mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The β-barrel domain has a possible function in either substrate recognition or maintaining structural integrity of the enzyme.
source: Notably, deletion of the N-terminal 80 or 95 residues abolished TibC heptosylation of TibA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating a possible function of the β-barrel domain in either substrate recognition or maintaining structural integrity of the enzyme.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of activity upon deletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The TibC catalytic domain contains two lobes linked by a long loop.
source: The catalytic domain contains two lobes (residues 98–195 and 218–406, respectively) linked by a long loop (residues 196–217).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A).

claim: The N-lobe of TibC contains β9–12, α1–4 and surrounding loops, adopting a compact Rossmann-like globular fold.
source: The N-lobe, containing β9–12, α1–4 and surrounding loops, adopts a compact Rossmann-like globular fold.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A).

claim: The β-sheet in the N-lobe of TibC is flanked by α-helices at one side but the β-barrel at the other side, differing from the classical Rossmann fold.
source: Different from the classical Rossmann fold that has α-helices flanking the central β-sheet, the β-sheet in the N-lobe is flanked by α-helices (α1–4) at one side but the β-barrel at the other side (Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A) and compared with classical Rossmann fold.

claim: The C-lobe of TibC features a central β-sheet sandwiched by α-helices, adopting a typical Rossmann fold.
source: The C-lobe (α5–11 and β13–18) features a central β-sheet (β13 and β16–18) sandwiched by α7/α8 at one side and α6/α11 at the other side, adopting a typical Rossmann fold.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A) and compared with typical Rossmann fold.

claim: The catalytic domain of TibC structurally more resembles the GT-B fold such as WaaC and MurG.
source: The catalytic domain of TibC structurally more resembles the GT-B fold such as WaaC and MurG, two bacterial glycosyltransferases involved in cell wall synthesis (Hu et al., 2003; Grizot et al., 2006), with its own distinctions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison (Figure 3B) and cited references (Hu et al., 2003; Grizot et al., 2006).

claim: The N-lobe of the TibC catalytic domain is not a typical Rossmann fold; its central β-sheet is four-stranded rather than six-stranded and also misses the flanking α-helices at one side.
source: One major difference is that the N-lobe of the TibC catalytic domain is not a typical Rossmann fold; its central β-sheet is four-stranded rather than six-stranded for a Rossmann fold and also misses the flanking α-helices at one side (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison with typical Rossmann fold (Figure 3B).

claim: The TibC β-hairpin thumb consists of β15, β16, and a four-residue hairpin loop projecting away from the globular C-lobe.
source: The β-hairpin thumb consists of β15, β16, and a four-residue hairpin loop projecting away from the globular C-lobe (Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A).

claim: Phe-265 and Val-266 at the tip of the β-hairpin thumb, together with a nearby Phe-368, contact the same set of residues from the adjacent protomer to form a hydrophobic cluster.
source: Phe-265 and Val-266 at the tip of the thumb, together with a nearby Phe-368 from the catalytic domain, contact the same set of residues from the adjacent protomer to form a hydrophobic cluster (Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 4A).

claim: TibC F368D mutant was largely insoluble.
source: TibC F368D mutant was largely insoluble.
evidence: Observed during protein expression and purification experiments.

claim: Both TibC F265D and V266D mutants eluted as a dimer from the gel filtration column.
source: Both F265D and V266D mutants eluted as a dimer from the gel filtration column (Figure 4B) and failed to catalyze TibA heptosylation in E. coli (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration chromatography (Figure 4B).

claim: TibC F265D and V266D mutants failed to catalyze TibA heptosylation in E. coli.
source: Both F265D and V266D mutants eluted as a dimer from the gel filtration column (Figure 4B) and failed to catalyze TibA heptosylation in E. coli (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycosylation assays (Figure 4C).

claim: The β-hairpin thumb is important for mediating the hand-in-hand association for assembly of an active TibC dodecamer.
source: These results highlight the importance of the β-hairpin thumb in mediating the hand-in-hand association for assembly of an active TibC dodecamer.
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data showing loss of dodecamer formation and activity (Figure 4B, C).

claim: The unique presence of two successive hydrophobic residues on TibC β-hairpin loop differs from other β-hairpin loops that are usually dominated by hydrophilic residues.
source: The data also explain the unique presence of two successive hydrophobic residues on TibC β-hairpin loop, which differs from other β-hairpin loops that are usually dominated by hydrophilic residues (Sibanda and Thornton, 1985).
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis and comparison with general β-hairpin loop characteristics (Sibanda and Thornton, 1985).

claim: The TibC iron-finger motif features two knuckles with long exposed loops capping and embellishing the C-lobe.
source: The other insertion module (residues -368) features two knuckles with long exposed loops capping and embellishing the C-lobe (Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A).

claim: Within the iron-finger motif, a ferric ion is tetrahedrally coordinated by four conserved cysteine residues (Cys-339, 342, 358, and 370 in TibC).
source: Within the module, a ferric ion is tetrahedrally coordinated by four conserved cysteine residues (Cys-339, 342, 358, and 370 in TibC) (Figure 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), analogous to the zinc-finger motif.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A) and conservation shown in alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The TibC iron-finger motif architecture belongs to the 1Fe-0S cluster.
source: This iron-finger motif lies ∼20 Å from the catalytic cleft (see below) and its architecture belongs to the 1Fe-0S cluster.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis and comparison with known metal clusters.

claim: The 1Fe-0S iron-finger motif is only observed once in rubredoxin protein found in sulfur-metabolizing bacteria and archaea.
source: Differing from the most common zinc-finger motif, the 1Fe-0S iron-finger motif is only observed once in rubredoxin protein found in sulfur-metabolizing bacteria and archaea (Lovenberg and Sobel, 1965; Adman et al., 1975).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Lovenberg and Sobel, 1965; Adman et al., 1975).

claim: In rubredoxin, the 1Fe-0S cluster acts as an electron transfer carrier.
source: In rubredoxin, the 1Fe-0S cluster acts as an electron transfer carrier (Sieker et al., 1994).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Sieker et al., 1994).

claim: The iron-finger motif in TibC does not seem to function in electron transfer.
source: The iron-finger motif in TibC, however, does not seem to function in electron transfer according to our structural and functional analyses.
evidence: Inferred from structural and functional analyses showing role in dodecamer assembly rather than electron transfer.

claim: Mutation of any of the four iron-coordinating cysteine residues resulted in a colorless TibC protein due to the loss of iron binding.
source: Notably, mutation of any of the four iron-coordinating cysteine residues resulted in a colorless TibC protein (Figure 5A) due to the loss of iron binding.
evidence: Demonstrated by visual observation of purified mutant proteins (Figure 5A).

claim: The four cysteine mutants of TibC eluted from the gel filtration column as heterogeneous interconverting oligomers with their sizes smaller than a dodecamer.
source: The four cysteine mutants eluted from the gel filtration column as heterogeneous interconverting oligomers with their sizes smaller than a dodecamer (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration chromatography (Figure 5B).

claim: The iron finger is required for maintaining structural integrity of the TibC dodecamer.
source: Thus, the iron finger is required for maintaining structural integrity of the TibC dodecamer.
evidence: Inferred from gel filtration data showing loss of dodecamer formation in iron-binding mutants (Figure 5B).

claim: The four iron binding-deficient mutants all failed to catalyze TibA heptosylation in the E. coli system.
source: Consistently, the four iron binding-deficient mutants all failed to catalyze TibA heptosylation in the E. coli system (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycosylation assays (Figure 5C).

claim: A portion of the iron-finger motif, together with several surface residues from the catalytic domain of one protomer, makes extensive contacts with the β-barrel and the catalytic domain of the other protomer in the back-to-back dimer.
source: Structurally, the iron-finger motif contributes to the back-to-back dimerization. A portion of the iron-finger motif, together with several surface residues from the catalytic domain of one protomer, makes extensive contacts with the β-barrel as well as the catalytic domain of the other protomer in the back-to-back dimer (Figure 5D).
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 5D).

claim: A symmetric interface is formed via the same kind of interactions between the two protomers in the back-to-back dimer.
source: A symmetric interface is formed via the same kind of interactions between the two protomers.
evidence: Directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 5D).

claim: Extensive polar and hydrophobic contacts occur at the back-to-back dimer interface, burying approximately 1467 Å2 solvent-accessible surface area of TibC.
source: Extensive polar and hydrophobic contacts occur at the interface (Figure 5D), burying ∼1467 Å2 solvent-accessible surface area of TibC (∼9% of the total surface areas).
evidence: Calculated from the crystal structure (Figure 5D).

claim: Dimerization via the large back-to-back interface provides building blocks for TibC dodecamer assembly.
source: Dimerization via this large interface provides building blocks for TibC dodecamer assembly.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis showing dimers as the basic unit for dodecamer formation.

claim: The TibC-ADP-D,D-heptose complex structure was obtained by soaking the sugar ligand into crystals of the catalytically inactive TibC D110A mutant.
source: This was accomplished by soaking the sugar ligand into crystals of the catalytically inactive TibC D110A mutant.
evidence: Described as the method used to obtain the ligand-bound structure.

claim: ADP-D,D-heptose was convincingly modeled into each protomer and a final model of 3.88 Å was obtained.
source: ADP-D,D-heptose was convincingly modeled into each protomer and a final model of 3.88 Å was obtained (Table 1).
evidence: Described as the result of structure determination with crystallographic statistics (Table 1).

claim: The 12 sugar ligands form an array of two parallel circles along the inner surface of the dodecamer ring and face towards the hollow center.
source: The 12 sugar ligands form an array of two parallel circles along the inner surface of the dodecamer ring and face towards the hollow center (Figure 6A).
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6A).

claim: ADP-D,D-heptose is located at the cleft between the two lobes of the catalytic domain.
source: ADP-D,D-heptose is located at the cleft between the two lobes of the catalytic domain (Figure 6B and Figure 3B).
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6B).

claim: The adenine heterocycle of ADP-D,D-heptose fits snugly into a hydrophilic pocket and its N1 atom bears a hydrogen bond contact with Arg-286 of TibC.
source: The adenine heterocycle fits snugly into a hydrophilic pocket and its N1 atom bears a hydrogen bond contact with Arg-286 of TibC (Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6B).

claim: The hydrogen bond contact between adenine N1 and Arg-286 is incompatible with a guanine due to its saturated N1, providing a structural basis for the specificity of TibC in using ADP-activated sugar donor.
source: The hydrogen bond contact, though weak, is incompatible with a guanine due to its saturated N1, providing a structural basis for the specificity of TibC in using ADP-activated sugar donor.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of the ligand binding site (Figure 6B).

claim: The heptose hydroxyl O4 forms a hydrogen bond with Trp-305 indolic N1.
source: Moreover, the heptose hydroxyl O4 forms a hydrogen bond with Trp-305 indolic N1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6B).

claim: The β-phosphate of ADP-D,D-heptose has strong interactions with Thr-226 and Lys-230 in the ligand-binding pocket of TibC.
source: The β-phosphate has strong interactions with Thr-226 and Lys-230 in the ligand-binding pocket of TibC.
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6B).

claim: Lys-230 is close to the heptose hydroxyl O5 and its positive charge could potentially alleviate the negative charge of β-phosphate, thereby facilitating nucleophilic attack of the heptose C1 by the substrate acceptor.
source: Lys-230 is also close to the heptose hydroxyl O5; its positive charge could potentially alleviate the negative charge of β-phosphate, thereby facilitating nucleophilic attack of the heptose C1 by the substrate acceptor.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of the catalytic site (Figure 6B).

claim: Asp-110 is the candidate catalytic base that activates the substrate acceptor.
source: Superimposition of the TibC sugar binding site with those of the GT-B glycosyltransferases WaaC and MurG identified Asp-110 as the candidate catalytic base that activates the substrate acceptor.
evidence: Identified by structural comparison with known GT-B glycosyltransferases (WaaC and MurG) and position near the anomeric hydroxyl (Figure 6B).

claim: Asp-110 is located close to the anomeric hydroxyl of heptose in the TibC–ADP-D,D-heptose complex structure.
source: Asp-110 is located close to the anomeric hydroxyl of heptose in the TibC–ADP-D,D-heptose complex structure (Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6B).

claim: All four sugar-binding residues (Arg-286, Trp-305, Thr-226, and Lys-230) as well as the catalytic base (Asp-110) are highly conserved in the BAHT family.
source: All four sugar-binding residues (Arg-286, Trp-305, Thr-226, and Lys-230) as well as the catalytic base (Asp-110) are highly conserved in the BAHT family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Alanine substitution of Asp-110, Arg-286, Trp-305, or Lys-230 in TibC all abolished or largely diminished TibA/AIDA-I heptosylation in E. coli.
source: Alanine substitution of Asp-110, Arg-286, Trp-305, or Lys-230 in TibC all abolished or largely diminished TibA/AIDA-I heptosylation in E. coli (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A); these point mutants also failed to support AIDA-I-mediated bacterial adhesion to HeLa cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by glycosylation assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: TibC point mutants (D110A, R286A, W305A, K230A) failed to support AIDA-I-mediated bacterial adhesion to HeLa cells.
source: Alanine substitution of Asp-110, Arg-286, Trp-305, or Lys-230 in TibC all abolished or largely diminished TibA/AIDA-I heptosylation in E. coli (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A); these point mutants also failed to support AIDA-I-mediated bacterial adhesion to HeLa cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bacterial adhesion assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The mutagenesis results confirm the functional importance of the heptosyltransferase activity of TibC and the BAHT family.
source: The results also confirm the functional importance of the heptosyltransferase activity of TibC and the BAHT family.
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data showing loss of glycosylation and adhesion function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: AAH accepts both ADP-D,D-heptose and ADP-L,D-heptose as the sugar donor despite a possible slight preference for the latter.
source: AAH accepts both ADP-D,D-heptose and ADP-L,D-heptose as the sugar donor despite a possible slight preference for the latter (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: TibC exhibited a high stereoselectivity for ADP-D,D-heptose.
source: In contrast, TibC exhibited a high stereoselectivity for ADP-D,D-heptose.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro enzymatic assays showing activity only with ADP-D,D-heptose (Figure 6C).

claim: Residue 300 in TibC (294 in AAH) is a possible structural determinant for sugar ligand stereoselectivity.
source: To reveal the underlying structural basis, we modeled the structure of sugar ligand-bound AAH using the TibC complex as the template and examined TibC/AAH residues within 5 Å from the sugar ligand (Figure 6D). This led to the identification of residue 300 in TibC (294 in AAH) as a possible structural determinant.
evidence: Identified by structural modeling and analysis (Figure 6D).

claim: In TibC, Pro-300 main-chain carbonyl oxygen forms two hydrogen bonds with D,D-heptose hydroxyl O4 and O6.
source: In TibC, residue 300 is a proline and its main-chain carbonyl oxygen forms two hydrogen bonds with D,D-heptose hydroxyl O4 and O6, respectively (Figure 6E).
evidence: Directly observed in the ligand-bound crystal structure (Figure 6E).

claim: The interaction between Pro-300 and hydroxyl O6 in D,D-heptose is incompatible with L,D-heptose due to the chiral inversion of C6 and the resulting spatial distance.
source: Notably, the latter interaction is incompatible with L,D-heptose due to the chiral inversion of C6 and the resulting spatial distance.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of ligand binding (Figure 6E).

claim: For AAH, the side-chain hydroxyl of Ser-294 can have a polar interaction with hydroxyl O6 in D,D-heptose or hydroxyl O7 in L,D-heptose, thereby capable of tolerating both sugar ligands.
source: For AAH, the side-chain hydroxyl of Ser-294 can have a polar interaction with hydroxyl O6 in D,D-heptose or hydroxyl O7 in L,D-heptose (Figure 6E), thereby capable of tolerating both sugar ligands.
evidence: Inferred from structural modeling (Figure 6E).

claim: TibC P300S mutant could use both ADP-D,D-heptose and ADP-L,D-heptose.
source: Consistent with these structural indications, TibC P300S mutant could use both ADP-D,D-heptose and ADP-L,D-heptose while AAH S294P mutant instead became selective for ADP-D,D-heptose (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).

claim: AAH S294P mutant became selective for ADP-D,D-heptose.
source: Consistent with these structural indications, TibC P300S mutant could use both ADP-D,D-heptose and ADP-L,D-heptose while AAH S294P mutant instead became selective for ADP-D,D-heptose (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Pro-300-mediated polar interaction is a critical structural determinant for TibC sugar ligand stereoselectivity.
source: Thus, Pro-300-mediated polar interaction is a critical structural determinant for TibC sugar ligand stereoselectivity.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis and mutagenesis experiments swapping stereoselectivity (Figure 6C, E).

claim: A TibC–TibA enzyme/substrate complex was purified by co-expression of the sugar binding-deficient TibC K230A mutant with TibA55-350 in E. coli.
source: We further succeeded in purifying a TibC–TibA enzyme/substrate complex by co-expression of the sugar binding-deficient TibC K230A mutant with TibA55-350 in E. coli.
evidence: Described as the method used to obtain the complex for cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The TibC–TibA complex eluted from the gel filtration column as a homogenous fraction with a size larger than the TibC dodecamer.
source: The complex eluted from the gel filtration column as a homogenous fraction with a size larger than the TibC dodecamer.
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration chromatography.

claim: The molecular weight of the TibC–TibA enzyme/substrate assembly was determined to be 750 kDa by analytical ultracentrifugation, matching well the composition of a TibC dodecamer and six TibA molecules.
source: The molecular weight of the giant enzyme/substrate assembly was determined to be 750 kDa by analytical ultracentrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), matching well the composition of a TibC dodecamer and six TibA molecules.
evidence: Demonstrated by analytical ultracentrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Averaging and refinement without classification from the whole dataset of 53,303 particles produced an electron density map of 9.7 Å in which the TibC12–TibA6 stoichiometry became immediately evident.
source: Averaging and refinement without classification from the whole dataset of 53,303 particles produced an electron density map of 9.7 Å in which the TibC12–TibA6 stoichiometry became immediately evident (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 7A).

claim: The TibA moiety in the cryo-EM reconstruction is slightly blurred and segmented, indicating a conformational heterogeneity.
source: In this low-resolution model, density agreeing well with the crystal structure of the TibC dodecamer could be clearly identified, but the TibA moiety is slightly blurred and segmented, indicating a conformational heterogeneity.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 7A).

claim: The reconstructed cryo-EM maps could be classified into two classes based on different features of the TibA density.
source: The reconstructed maps could be further classified into two classes based on different features of the TibA density (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D classification of cryo-EM data (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Two cryo-EM maps of higher resolution at 8.2 Å and 8.9 Å were reconstructed by averaging 35,300 and 18,003 sorted particles, respectively.
source: Two maps of higher resolution at 8.2 Å and 8.9 Å were then reconstructed by averaging 35,300 and 18,003 sorted particles, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by cryo-EM reconstruction after classification (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: The two classified cryo-EM maps indicate two major conformational states of the TibC–TibA enzyme/substrate complex in the absence of the sugar donor.
source: These analyses indicate two major conformational states of the TibC–TibA enzyme/substrate complex in the absence of the sugar donor.
evidence: Inferred from cryo-EM classification showing two distinct conformations (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: The 8.9 Å EM map fits remarkably well with crystal structures of TibA55-350 and the TibC dodecamer.
source: The 8.9 Å EM map fits remarkably well with crystal structures of TibA55-350 (PDB ID code: 4Q1Q) (Lu et al., 2014) and the TibC dodecamer (Figure 7B), allowing for reliable atomic model docking.
evidence: Demonstrated by fitting crystal structures into cryo-EM map (Figure 7B) with cited TibA structure (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: The cross-correlation coefficient for TibA in the final resting state model is 0.76.
source: The cross-correlation coefficient (CCC) for TibA in the final model is 0.76 (only a small N-terminal portion of TibA55-350 is out of the density).
evidence: Calculated from model fitting to cryo-EM density (Figure 7B).

claim: Six TibA55-350 molecules are distributed along the inner surface of the TibC dodecamer ring and share its sixfold axis.
source: The reconstruction revealed that six TibA55-350 molecules are distributed along the inner surface of the TibC dodecamer ring and share its sixfold axis (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 7C).

claim: Each TibA55-350 binds to two TibC protomers of a back-to-back dimer.
source: Importantly, each TibA55-350 binds to two TibC protomers of a back-to-back dimer, suggesting that two enzyme molecules are responsible for catalyzing full heptosylation of one TibA substrate.
evidence: Demonstrated by cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 7C).

claim: Two enzyme molecules are responsible for catalyzing full heptosylation of one TibA substrate.
source: Importantly, each TibA55-350 binds to two TibC protomers of a back-to-back dimer, suggesting that two enzyme molecules are responsible for catalyzing full heptosylation of one TibA substrate.
evidence: Inferred from the cryo-EM structure showing one TibA bound to two TibC protomers (Figure 7C).

claim: In the resting state, Ser-176 is the closest sugar acceptor situated at the entrance of the catalytic cleft of one TibC protomer, but the distance to the catalytic base exceeds 20 Å.
source: Ser-176 is the closest sugar acceptor situated at the entrance of the catalytic cleft of one TibC protomer (TibC-A), but the distance to the catalytic base exceeds 20 Å (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Measured from the resting state cryo-EM model (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).

claim: The 8.9 Å TibC–TibA dodecamer/hexamer complex model represents a sugar transfer incompetent state, designated as the resting state.
source: Thus, the 8.9 Å TibC–TibA dodecamer/hexamer complex model represents a sugar transfer incompetent state, designated hereafter as the resting state.
evidence: Inferred from the large distance between substrate and catalytic base (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).

claim: The spiral shaft of TibA β-helix adopts a trend roughly parallel to the sixfold axis of the dodecamer.
source: Moreover, the spiral shaft of TibA β-helix adopts a trend roughly parallel to the sixfold axis of the dodecamer which, together with the patterned solenoid-like surface distribution of heptosylation sites on TibA (Lu et al., 2014), indicates a possible screw propelling-like mechanism for processive heptosylation of TibA by the dodecamer ring.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure (Figure 7C).

claim: The arrangement of TibA in the complex indicates a possible screw propelling-like mechanism for processive heptosylation of TibA by the dodecamer ring.
source: Moreover, the spiral shaft of TibA β-helix adopts a trend roughly parallel to the sixfold axis of the dodecamer which, together with the patterned solenoid-like surface distribution of heptosylation sites on TibA (Lu et al., 2014), indicates a possible screw propelling-like mechanism for processive heptosylation of TibA by the dodecamer ring.
evidence: Inferred from the structural arrangement and cited heptosylation site distribution (Lu et al., 2014).

claim: The TibA moiety in the 8.2 Å EM map had a few degrees of bending with a protrusion into the catalytic center of one TibC protomer.
source: The static X-ray structures of TibC dodecamer and TibA55-350 were also docked into the 8.2 Å EM map, but the TibA moiety had a few degrees of bending with a protrusion into the catalytic center of one TibC protomer (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Observed when fitting crystal structures into the 8.2 Å cryo-EM map (Figure 7A, B, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).

claim: The extra protruding density in the 8.2 Å map was tentatively interpreted as the TibA loop bearing the sugar acceptor Ser-176.
source: The extra protruding density could not be appropriately fit despite extensive attempts at possible solutions. The heterogeneity observed in the cryo-EM image likely reflects the dynamic catalytic motions; the protruding density was tentatively interpreted as the TibA loop bearing the sugar acceptor Ser-176.
evidence: Inferred from the cryo-EM density and supported by MD simulation (Figure 7B, D, E).

claim: Molecular dynamics simulation of a resting state TibC2–TibA55-350 trimer supported the interpretation of the protruding density.
source: This interpretation was supported by molecular dynamics (MD) simulation of a resting state TibC2–TibA55-350 trimer.
evidence: Demonstrated by MD simulation showing loop protrusion (Figure 7D, E).

claim: In the 400 ps steered MD simulation, pulling Ser-176 in TibA55-350 towards the heptose led to a proportional increase in the cross-correlation coefficient.
source: In the 400 ps steered MD simulation, pulling Ser-176 in TibA55-350 towards the heptose led to a proportional increase in the CCC (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: Demonstrated by steered MD simulation (Figure 7D, E).

claim: A subsequent 20 ns unbiased MD simulation produced an ensemble of TibA models that matched the EM density with a best overall CCC value of 0.87.
source: A subsequent 20 ns unbiased MD simulation produced an ensemble of TibA models that matched the EM density with a best overall CCC value of 0.87 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by unbiased MD simulation (Figure 7B).

claim: The protruding loop was assigned to residues 170–180 of TibA, resulting from disruption of a local β-strand within these residues.
source: The protruding loop was assigned to residues 170–180 of TibA, resulting from disruption of a local β-strand within these residues.
evidence: Determined by MD simulation and fitting to cryo-EM density (Figure 7B, E).

claim: The loop protrusion placed Ser-176 into a position ready for attacking the sugar donor in one TibC protomer.
source: The loop placed Ser-176 into a position ready for attacking the sugar donor in one TibC protomer (TibC-A) (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by the post-MD model fitted into cryo-EM density (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).

claim: The 'protrusion' state of TibA was designated as the catalytically competent active state.
source: This 'protrusion' state of TibA was designated as the catalytically competent active state.
evidence: Defined based on the positioning of Ser-176 near the catalytic site (Figure 7C).

claim: In the active state, only one of the two enzyme molecules in the dimer can be productive in transferring the sugar onto TibA at a time.
source: Notably, the other TibC protomer (TibC-B) in the back-to-back dimer and its possible substrate acceptor appeared to be in the resting state (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C,D), suggesting that only one of the two enzyme molecules in the dimer can be productive in transferring the sugar onto TibA at a time.
evidence: Inferred from the active state cryo-EM structure showing asymmetry in the dimer (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C, D).

claim: The active state structure, reconstructed from two-thirds of the total particles, probably contains the majority of representative conformational stages in the catalytic process.
source: The active state structure, which was reconstructed from two-thirds of the total particles, probably contains the majority of representative conformational stages in the catalytic process and therefore is used to represent the overall structure of the TibC–TibA dodecamer/hexamer complex (Figure 7C).
evidence: Inferred from the particle distribution in classification (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: The selection of a double-layered ring with a large hollow channel is advantageous and provides a favorable environment for cooperative catalysis in a structurally economical manner.
source: The selection of a double-layered ring with a large hollow channel is advantageous and provides a favorable environment for cooperative catalysis in a structurally economical manner.
evidence: Inferred from the structural architecture and functional properties.

claim: Assembly of the dodecamer into a ring can reduce the solvent-accessible surface area and renders a stable enzymatic machinery complex beneficial to efficient catalysis.
source: Assembly of the dodecamer into a ring can reduce the solvent-accessible surface area and renders a stable enzymatic machinery complex beneficial to efficient catalysis.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis and general principles of protein assembly.

claim: The spatial arrangement of the back-to-back TibC dimer binding to different glycosylation sites in one TibA suggests a divalent catalysis is probably contributing to the high catalytic efficiency required for hyperglycosylation.
source: Moreover, the spatial arrangement of the back-to-back TibC dimer, binding to the different glycosylation sites in one TibA, suggests a divalent catalysis is also probably contributing to the high catalytic efficiency required for hyperglycosylation.
evidence: Inferred from the cryo-EM structure showing one TibA bound to two TibC protomers (Figure 7C).

claim: The dodecamer/hexamer enzyme/substrate complex with six symmetric units may represent a best compromise between structural economy and catalytic cooperativity/efficiency.
source: Thus, the dodecamer/hexamer enzyme/substrate complex with six symmetric units may represent a best compromise between structural economy and catalytic cooperativity/efficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the overall structural and functional analysis.

claim: The TibC complex is more permeable than other macromolecular assemblies with large interior volumes such as ferritin and multimeric chaperones/proteases, with 12 tilted grooves extending from outside to the interior chamber.
source: The TibC complex, compared with other macromolecular assemblies with large interior volumes such as ferritin and multimeric chaperones/proteases, is more permeable with 12 titled grooves extending from outside to the interior chamber.
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison with other macromolecular assemblies.

claim: The grooves in TibC are optimally imbedded and close to the catalytic center, allowing for easy access of ADP-heptose from outside into the TibC particle.
source: These grooves are optimally imbedded and close to the catalytic center, allowing for easy access of ADP-heptose from outside into the TibC particle.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of the dodecamer architecture.

claim: The catalytic center is structurally best accessible from the interior, where TibA is located and can readily deliver the to-be-glycosylated serine by loop protrusion.
source: The catalytic center, on the other hand, is structurally best accessible from the interior, where TibA is located and can readily deliver the to-be-glycosylated serine by loop protrusion.
evidence: Inferred from the cryo-EM structure showing TibA inside the dodecamer ring (Figure 7C).

claim: The energy used to drive the rotation and shuttle motion of the TibA substrate is partially derived from breakdown of the ADP-heptose glycosidic bond occurring during catalysis.
source: We further speculate that the energy used to drive the rotation and shuttle motion of the TibA substrate is partially derived from breakdown of the ADP-heptose glycosidic bond occurring during catalysis.
evidence: Speculated based on the structural arrangement and catalytic mechanism.

claim: The iron-finger motif does not fulfill the previously defined function of serving as an electron carrier in rubredoxin protein.
source: The iron-finger motif does not fulfill the previously defined function of serving as an electron carrier in rubredoxin protein.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical and structural studies showing role in dodecamer assembly rather than electron transfer.

claim: The iron-finger motif, adopting a topological fold similar to the zinc-finger motif, follows a right-handed helical path in binding to TibA β-helix, which is analogous to DNA binding by zinc-finger motifs.
source: Interestingly, the iron-finger motif, adopting a topological fold similar to the zinc-finger motif, follows a right-handed helical path in binding to TibA β-helix, which is analogous to DNA binding by zinc-finger motifs.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of the TibC-TibA complex and comparison with zinc-finger-DNA interactions.

claim: The recognition specificity and the interaction strength of the iron-finger motif have been precisely tuned during macromolecular evolution so that specific substrate recognition, sliding of the TibA β-helix along the reaction channel, and efficient protrusion of the TibA loop can all occur in a catalytically productive manner.
source: In addition, the recognition specificity and the interaction strength of this motif will have been precisely tuned during macromolecular evolution so that specific substrate recognition, sliding of the TibA β-helix along the reaction channel, and efficient protrusion of the TibA loop can all occur in a catalytically productive manner.
evidence: Speculated based on the structural and functional properties of the iron-finger motif.

claim: Protein glycosylation is one of the most abundant post-translational modifications in all domains of life.
source: Protein glycosylation is one of the most abundant post-translational modifications in all domains of life (Spiro, 2002).
evidence: Cited from previous review (Spiro, 2002).

claim: Protein glycosylation in bacteria is often associated with pathogen virulence and immune modulation.
source: Recent studies have appreciated protein glycosylation in bacteria, which is often associated with pathogen virulence and immune modulation (Szymanski and Wren, 2005; Abu-Qarn et al., 2008; Nothaft and Szymanski, 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Szymanski and Wren, 2005; Abu-Qarn et al., 2008; Nothaft and Szymanski, 2010).

claim: Flagella glycosylation is found in many bacteria species including Campylobacter jejuni, Helicobacter pylori, Clostridium spp. and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, contributing to bacterial locomotion or virulence.
source: For instance, flagella glycosylation is found in many bacteria species including Campylobacter jejuni, Helicobacter pylori, Clostridium spp. and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, contributing to bacterial locomotion or virulence (Schirm et al., 2003; Nothaft and Szymanski, 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Schirm et al., 2003; Nothaft and Szymanski, 2010).

claim: Secreted effectors from enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) and related enteric pathogens harbor an arginine N-acetylglucosamine transferase activity that modifies host death-domain proteins and is essential for bacterial colonization in infected mice.
source: Recently, we and others have shown that secreted effectors from enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) and related enteric pathogens harbor an arginine N-acetylglucosamine transferase activity that modifies host death-domain proteins and is essential for bacterial colonization in infected mice (Li et al., 2013; Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Li et al., 2013; Pearson et al., 2013).

claim: Autotransporters represent the largest family of bacterial virulence factors.
source: Autotransporters, representing the largest family of bacterial virulence factors, share a similar structural organization containing a signal peptide followed by a functional passenger domain and a C-terminal β-barrel translocation domain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about autotransporters.

claim: Autotransporters play a critical role in diverse aspects of bacterial physiology including proteolytic digestion of host proteins, biofilm formation, adhesion and invasion of host cells, and intracellular motility.
source: Autotransporters play a critical role in diverse aspects of bacterial physiology including proteolytic digestion of host proteins, biofilm formation, adhesion and invasion of host cells, and intracellular motility (Henderson et al., 2004; Lazar Adler et al., 2011; Wells et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Henderson et al., 2004; Lazar Adler et al., 2011; Wells et al., 2007).

claim: AIDA-I from diffusely adhering E. coli (DAEC) 2787 and TibA from enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) H10407 are glycosylated in their passenger domains.
source: A subfamily of autotransporters, including AIDA-I (adhesin involved in diffuse adherence) from diffusely adhering E. coli (DAEC) 2787 (Benz and Schmidt, 1989) and TibA from enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) H10407 (Elsinghorst and Weitz, 1994), are glycosylated in their passenger domains (Lindenthal and Elsinghorst, 1999; Benz and Schmidt, 2001; Sherlock et al., 2006), which functions in bacterial autoaggregation and adhesion to host cells (Benz and Schmidt, 1989; Sherlock et al., 2004; Charbonneau and Mourez, 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Benz and Schmidt, 1989; Elsinghorst and Weitz, 1994; Lindenthal and Elsinghorst, 1999; Benz and Schmidt, 2001; Sherlock et al., 2006).

claim: Glycosylation of AIDA-I and TibA functions in bacterial autoaggregation and adhesion to host cells.
source: A subfamily of autotransporters, including AIDA-I (adhesin involved in diffuse adherence) from diffusely adhering E. coli (DAEC) 2787 (Benz and Schmidt, 1989) and TibA from enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) H10407 (Elsinghorst and Weitz, 1994), are glycosylated in their passenger domains (Lindenthal and Elsinghorst, 1999; Benz and Schmidt, 2001; Sherlock et al., 2006), which functions in bacterial autoaggregation and adhesion to host cells (Benz and Schmidt, 1989; Sherlock et al., 2004; Charbonneau and Mourez, 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Benz and Schmidt, 1989; Sherlock et al., 2004; Charbonneau and Mourez, 2007).

claim: AIDA-I and TibA-like autotransporters are present in diverse bacterial species.
source: AIDA-I and TibA-like autotransporters are present in diverse bacterial species.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Previous studies carried out in the ectopic system indicate a role for AAH in DAEC and its ETEC homologue TibC in AIDA-I and TibA glycosylation.
source: Previous studies carried out in the ectopic system (Benz and Schmidt, 2001; Moormann et al., 2002) indicate a role for AAH (autotransporter adhesin heptosyltransferase) in DAEC and its ETEC homologue TibC in AIDA-I and TibA glycosylation.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Benz and Schmidt, 2001; Moormann et al., 2002).

claim: AAH and TibC harbor no sequence homology to known glycosyltransferases.
source: However, AAH and TibC harbor no sequence homology to known glycosyltransferases and there has been no biochemical evidence demonstrating their glycosyltransferase activity.
evidence: Stated as the knowledge gap that motivated this study.

claim: AAH is a bona fide heptosyltransferase belonging to a large bacterial autotransporter heptosyltransferase (BAHT) family.
source: In a separate parallel study (Lu et al., 2014) we showed that AAH is a bona fide heptosyltransferase belonging to a large bacterial autotransporter heptosyltransferase (BAHT) family.
evidence: Cited from parallel study (Lu et al., 2014).
